parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a member of the platform's airspace desk. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day on the airspace desk, from the moment you start until you finish?
I don't know.
Let's start with just the very beginning of your shift—what is the first thing you look at or do when you sit down?
I don't know.
What was the worst day you've had at work in the last few months, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.
Is there anything in your work today that you check by hand because you don't fully trust it?
I don't know.
When you think about a new software service being built for your desk, what are you most afraid it might get wrong?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace by working on the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. What worries me is that closures can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and they are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.
When a closure comes into force or gets amended while drones are already in the air, what exactly do you need to know right away?

When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and closures are often amended during the day, for example when an area is widened or an end time moves.
What specifically makes up that "disruption" across customers—what details can or should you see, given that each company's operations are private?
I don't know.
Who hands information or work to you, and who do you hand your work off to?
I don't know.
Could you tell me more about the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones grouping them—how do those get created or changed?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which consists of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I don't know how the network of flight corridors and zones get created or changed.
When something goes wrong in the airspace or with a site, what do you need to know right afterward?
I don't know.
How do you interact with the dispatchers or fleet technicians at the customer companies, if at all?

I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations. I don't know how I interact with dispatchers or fleet technicians at the customer companies, if at all.
How do the closures announced by the authorities reach you, and what do you have to do to enter them?
I don't know how the closures announced by the authorities reach me. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
You mentioned that sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time—how does that affect your work on the airspace desk?

Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I keep the shared picture of the airspace, including the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities.
Are there any other details about the flight corridors, zones, sites, or closures that are important to your work?

The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce planned closures with start and end times, as well as sudden closures that apply at once. These closures are frequently amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.
What else can you tell me about the sites and the flight corridors between them, such as how they are used or shared?

Drones fly along corridors between named sites. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I keep the shared picture of the airspace, including the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them.
Who owns or uses the named sites—are they shared among companies or specific to each company?
I don't know.
Can you tell me anything more about the zones that group corridors and sites, versus the prohibited zones defined by the authorities?
The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited. I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them.
Do closures apply to specific corridors, sites, or zones, or are they defined in another way?
I don't know.
What else is part of your job or responsibilities on the airspace desk that we haven't touched on yet?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which covers the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
